title: Reed strength and mouthpieces, and small-time New Orleans jobs
summary: Good players used reeds of 2.5 to 3 with a medium open mouthpiece; Kelly mentions bingo-party jobs with Joe Clancy.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: I want to ask you some technical things, since you sold instruments. Oh, yeah. And reeds and all that. How hard a reed would people use in those days?

Most musicians, Dick, would actually use, most of the good players would use two and a half to three. Some extremists would use four, real hard reeds, but most of the guys would play a two and a half to three. And, to get the right sound, most of them used a medium open lay mouthpiece. Again, some of the guys would use. It depended on how, depended on how, how they wanted to sound. You know, mouthpiece is really, if you have your choice between a good horn and a bad mouthpiece and a good mouthpiece and a bad horn, you better take the mouthpiece. Mm-hm. Red Bowman was with him, Ellis Stratikas, the trombonist from Galaxia was with him, and no one was a friend of mine. They were around the store all the time, and that's how I got to know, so I was talking on the other hand. But I played with little bands like that. You know a guy, a butcher, like Joe Clancy, he booked jobs, he was a drummer, and he, I played with him, and the piano player, we sometimes used to play for bingo parties, all kind of things. At that time, they had to have music for nearly everything. Go ahead and ask me some of them.
